w: The first national park east of the Mississippi, proclaimed in 1916 as Sieur de Monts National Monument, renamed Lafayette in 1919 and Acadia in 1929. It holds Cadillac Mountain, the tallest peak on the US Atlantic coast, plus glacial granite domes and Rockefeller's network of carriage roads.
s: The first national park east of the Mississippi
_facts: Established 1916 as Sieur de Monts National Monument, renamed Acadia in 1929
First national park east of the Mississippi River
Contains Cadillac Mountain, tallest peak on the US Atlantic coast
Carriage road network financed by John D. Rockefeller Jr.

w: At just under 1,530 feet, this is the highest point within 25 miles of the Atlantic shore anywhere between Nova Scotia's Cape Breton Highlands and peaks in Mexico. For part of the year it earns the title of the first place in the continental US to see the sunrise.
s: First US sunrise, most of the year
_facts: Elevation nearly 1,530 feet, highest point in Hancock County
Highest point within 25 miles of the Atlantic shore between Cape Breton and Mexico
Seasonally the first spot in the continental US to see sunrise
Located within Acadia National Park on Mount Desert Island

a: 26 Mount Desert Street / Sieur de Monts Spring
w: Led by a Wabanaki-majority board, this museum centers the heritage of the Wabanaki Confederacy - Maliseet, Mi'kmaq, Passamaquoddy and Penobscot peoples - across two sites: a downtown Bar Harbor gallery and a historic trailside building at Sieur de Monts Spring, one of Maine's first purpose-built museum structures.
s: Wabanaki heritage, told by Wabanaki voices
_facts: Wabanaki-majority Board of Trustees
Two locations: downtown Bar Harbor and Sieur de Monts Spring in Acadia
Sieur de Monts building is a rare Mediterranean-inspired Maine structure on the NRHP
One of only two privately-operated trailside museums in the National Park system

w: Built in 1875 midway between Mount Desert Island and the Schoodic Peninsula, this lighthouse is unusual in coastal Maine: a square tower projects straight up through the middle of the square keeper's house. It still flashes red every 40 seconds as an active aid to navigation on Frenchman Bay.
s: A lighthouse tower rising through its keeper's house
_facts: Built 1875 on Egg Rock, Frenchman Bay
Square tower projects through the keeper's house roof
Flashes red every 40 seconds
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1988

w: Opposed to cars on Mount Desert Island, John D. Rockefeller Jr. personally oversaw this motor-free road network built 1919-1931, including sixteen granite bridges and two gatehouses. Listed on the National Register in 1979, the paths now carry walkers and cyclists in summer, skiers in winter.
_facts: Built 1919-1931, overseen personally by John D. Rockefeller Jr.
Includes sixteen granite bridges and two gatehouses
Closed to motor vehicles by design
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979

w: Carved by the Wisconsin Ice Sheet, this 187-acre tarn holds some of the clearest water in Maine, with visibility recorded as deep as 61 feet. The Bubbles, two rounded glacial hills, rise above its northeastern shore; swimming is banned since the pond supplies drinking water to the village of Seal Harbor.
_facts: 187 acres, up to 150 feet deep, formed by the Wisconsin Ice Sheet
Visibility recorded up to 61 feet, deepest readings in Maine
The Bubbles (North and South) rise above the northeast shore
Swimming banned - the pond supplies Seal Harbor's drinking water

w: Fifty-five acres on Frenchman's Bay give broad views across to the mountains of Mount Desert Island and over Lamoine's working waterfront. Quieter than Acadia across the water, it is run by Maine's Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry.
s: Quiet views of Acadia across Frenchman Bay
_facts: 55 acres on the shore of Frenchman's Bay
Views of Mount Desert Island's mountains
Overlooks Lamoine's working waterfront
Managed by Maine's Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry
